title: The quality technique: planning, control and project acceptance
blurb: Describe the three steps of the PRINCE2 quality management technique and what project acceptance achieves.
question: What does acceptance of the project product typically transfer, and to whom?

teach.body: Formally: the PRINCE2 technique for the quality practice has three parts: quality planning, quality control and project acceptance. In plain English: decide what good looks like and how it will be checked, check the products as they are made, then formally hand the finished project product over so the users can own it. The technique gives the practice a repeatable way of working on any project.

steps.label: Quality planning
steps.sub: PPD in, QMA and product descriptions out

steps.label: Project acceptance
steps.sub: ownership passes to the board for users

teach.h: Don't mix up the two lists of three
teach.caption: The guidance names three elements of quality management; the technique ends with project acceptance instead of quality assurance.

teach.body: The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria, documented in the project product description during starting up, are a primary input. From them come product descriptions and the quality management approach. The approach should concentrate on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported, with a short explanation of how quality planning was done.

Teams carry out the quality methods named in the product descriptions, such as testing, inspection, prototyping or trials. Each activity and its result is recorded in the quality register, which supplies information for end stage reports and the end project report. If a product fails a check but is expected to pass after rework, repeating the check can be reasonable.

Acceptance of a project product typically transfers ownership of, or responsibility for, the product from the project or the supplier to the project board on behalf of the user. In closing a project, the 'confirm project acceptance' activity makes sure the products have passed to the operational and maintenance environment, either in one release or in phases.

children.label:
Project board,
on behalf of the user

teach.body: Ravensmoor Academy Trust is adding a science block. In starting up, senior user and head teacher Priya Nandakumar sets acceptance criteria such as gas safety certification and lab benches at the agreed height. Project manager Gareth Lloyd writes the quality management approach and product descriptions. The contractor's team tests each lab and records results in the quality register. When everything has passed, the board confirms acceptance on behalf of staff and pupils, and ownership of the block moves from the contractor to the trust.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) The technique's third step is project ACCEPTANCE, not quality assurance. (2) Acceptance transfers ownership to the project BOARD on behalf of the user, not to the supplier or the business layer. (3) The QMA should focus on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported, not be a long history of planning.

items: Technique: quality planning, quality control, project acceptance.
Planning: PPD expectations and criteria are a primary input; QMA focuses on how quality control will work.
Control: carry out methods, record activity and result in the quality register.
Acceptance transfers ownership from the project or supplier to the board on behalf of the user.

summary: You can now describe the three steps of the quality technique and what each produces. You can also explain that project acceptance passes ownership to the project board on behalf of the user, and avoid confusing the technique with the three elements of quality management.

A.q: Which are the three steps of the PRINCE2 quality management technique?
options: Quality planning, quality control, quality assurance
Quality planning, quality control, project acceptance
Develop, check, maintain, confirm
Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
A.why: The quality technique has three parts: quality planning, quality control and project acceptance (manual 8.3.1).

whyNot.0: These are the three elements of quality management in the guidance, not the technique.
whyNot.2: These are the business case technique steps.
whyNot.3: These are the issues technique steps.

A.q: What does acceptance of a project product typically transfer?
options: Funding responsibility from the executive to the business layer
Quality tolerance from the project manager to the team manager
Ownership from the project or supplier to the board for the user
Responsibility for benefits from the senior user to the supplier
A.why: Acceptance typically transfers ownership or responsibility for the product from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (manual 8.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Funding stays with the executive; acceptance concerns the product.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are delegated through plans and work packages, not by acceptance.
whyNot.3: The senior user remains responsible for the continued realization of benefits after the project.

A.q: Which is a primary input to quality planning?
options: The end stage report from the previous stage
The quality register for the current stage
The checkpoint reports from team managers
The project product description from starting up
A.why: The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria, in the PPD produced in starting up, are a primary input (manual 8.3.1.1.1).

whyNot.0: End stage reports review a completed stage; they are not the primary input to quality planning.
whyNot.1: The quality register records quality control results, which come after planning.
whyNot.2: Checkpoint reports describe work package progress.

B.q: What should the quality management approach focus on, according to the quality technique?
options: How quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported
A detailed history of every quality planning meeting held so far
The specific risks to each product, with their owners and actions
The benefits each product will deliver after the project closes
B.why: The QMA should focus on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported, with a concise explanation of how quality planning occurred (manual 8.3.1.1.3).

whyNot.1: The QMA gives a concise explanation of planning, not a detailed history.
whyNot.2: Specific risks belong in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Benefits belong in the business case and benefits management approach.

B.q:
Which two statements about the quality technique are correct?
1. Quality control records activities and results in the quality register.
2. Project acceptance is carried out by the quality assurance function.
3. Project acceptance makes the project board the owner on behalf of the user.
4. Quality planning starts after the first delivery stage.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Quality control results are recorded in the quality register (1), and acceptance transfers ownership to the board on behalf of the user (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: quality assurance is independent of the project and does not accept the product.
whyNot.1: Both are false: QA does not accept products, and planning starts with the PPD in starting up.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: quality planning begins with the PPD in starting up and continues in initiation.

B.q: During quality control, a heating unit fails its pressure test. The team expects it to pass after replacing a valve. What does the technique allow?
options: Repeating the test and recording the results
Accepting the unit and noting the fault
Removing the test from the product description
Passing the unit to quality assurance to approve
B.why: If a product fails a quality control activity and is expected to pass, it may be reasonable to repeat the activity; results are recorded in the quality register.

whyNot.1: A product that has not met its specifications should not be accepted as if it had.
whyNot.2: Changing a baselined product description needs change control, and would not fix the product.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance reviews the controls; it does not approve individual products.

C.q: Which process confirms project acceptance, and where do the accepted products go?
options: Controlling a stage; to the quality assurance function
Managing product delivery; to the team manager who built them
Closing a project; to the operational and maintenance environment
Directing a project; back to the project's suppliers for support
C.why: The 'confirm project acceptance' activity in closing a project ensures the products have passed to the operational and maintenance environment (manual 19.4.3).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage receives completed work packages; QA does not take ownership of products.
whyNot.1: Managing product delivery produces products; acceptance of the project product is confirmed in closing.
whyNot.3: Directing a project authorizes closure; products go to operational use, not back to suppliers.

C.q: A project delivers its products in three releases. How does this affect project acceptance?
options: Acceptance happens once, after the final release
Products may be passed over in several releases
Each release needs a separate project board
Releases are accepted by quality assurance
C.why: Products may be passed to operational use as a single release at the end or in several releases if the project approach includes phased delivery.

whyNot.0: Phased delivery means products can be handed over in several releases.
whyNot.2: One project board directs the project throughout.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance is independent of the project and does not accept products.

C.q: Which step of the technique produces the product descriptions, and which step uses them to check products?
options: Project acceptance; quality planning
Quality control; project acceptance
Quality assurance; quality control
Quality planning; quality control
C.why: Quality planning produces product descriptions and the QMA; quality control carries out the methods they specify.

whyNot.0: Acceptance comes last and does not write product descriptions.
whyNot.1: Quality control uses product descriptions; acceptance transfers ownership.
whyNot.2: Quality assurance is not a step of the technique.

reteach.title: Buying a new-build house
reteach.question: When does the house become yours?

blocks.body: Before building, you and the builder agree the specification (planning). During the build, inspectors check foundations, wiring and plumbing and record the results (control). At completion, you inspect, sign and receive the keys: ownership moves from the builder to you (acceptance). In PRINCE2, the keys go to the project board on behalf of the users.

blocks.text: The building inspector's audit of the builder's checks is quality assurance, but it is not a step of the technique.

explain.body: The technique is quality planning, quality control and project acceptance.

test.q: Which is the final step of the quality technique?
options: Quality assurance
Quality review
Project acceptance
Project closure
test.why: The technique ends with project acceptance, after quality planning and quality control.

whyNot.0: Quality assurance is one of the three elements of quality management, not a technique step.
whyNot.1: A review is one kind of quality method used within quality control.
whyNot.3: Closure is a process; acceptance is the technique step.

explain.body: The PPD's expectations and acceptance criteria, from starting up, are a primary input to quality planning.

test.q: In which process are the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria produced?
options: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Controlling a stage
Closing a project
test.why: They are documented in the project product description produced in starting up a project.

whyNot.0: Initiation uses them to produce the QMA and product descriptions.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage applies quality controls to work packages.

explain.body: Quality control carries out methods and records activity and result in the quality register.

test.q: Where does quality control record its activities and results?
options: Lessons log
Product register
Risk register
Quality register
test.why: Quality control activities and their results are recorded in the quality register.

whyNot.1: The product register lists products and their status.

explain.body: Ownership passes from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user.

test.q: On whose behalf does the project board take ownership at project acceptance?
options: The user
The supplier
The business layer
The project manager
test.why: Acceptance typically transfers ownership from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user.

whyNot.1: Ownership passes from the supplier, not to it.
whyNot.2: The business layer commissions the project; acceptance is on behalf of the user.
whyNot.3: The PM manages the project; the PM does not take ownership of the product.
